# RL Lab

**Status:** Draft · **Last updated:** 2026-10-18

## The problem
I want to understand reinforcement learning, where an agent learns by trial and error from rewards, well enough to build it myself. Tutorials hand over working code, so when an agent fails to learn I can't tell why. Building small worlds, and writing the learning methods for them myself, is how I'll get that understanding.

## Who it's for
Me: comfortable in Python and new to reinforcement learning beyond tutorials. I'll work on it in evenings and at weekends.

## Goals
1. I understand each core learning method well enough to write it myself and explain why it works or fails.
2. Each world teaches one idea. Snake teaches learning the value of each move. Fish fleeing a ball teach smooth movement with limited sight. Predator and prey teach two sides learning against each other.
3. I can tell real learning from luck. Every trained agent is measured against a simple hand-written player and against a trusted library version of the same method.
4. I can see what an agent learned, through replays of trained agents and a learning curve for every run.
5. Experiments can be compared. Each training run is saved with its settings, so I can see what a change did.

## Constraints
- A laptop for normal use, and each world trains in under about an hour. A few dollars of rented computing is fine if a world truly needs it.
- Spare time only: a few weeks per world, and no deadline.
- No outside data. Every world produces its own experience.

## What success looks like
- The Snake agent clearly beats a hand-written "head toward the food" player.
- Trained fish survive clearly longer than fish that just swim straight away from the ball.
- In predator and prey, I've seen the two sides chase each other in circles, and seen training against past opponents settle it.
- My own learning methods score close to the library versions on the same world.

## What we're betting on
- The worlds are rich enough to show each idea, yet small enough to train on a laptop in under an hour.
- Writing the methods myself, with a library as an answer key, teaches more than either alone.
- Predator and prey can be built on top of the fish tank instead of from scratch.

## Not doing
- Learning from screen pixels. Agents get simple measurements such as positions and distances, which keeps training laptop-sized.
- Evolving populations of agents. It's a different branch of the field.
- 3D worlds or physics engines. Two dimensions keep the focus on learning.
- A public demo or web app. Replays are for me.
- Fish competing with each other in the tank. They share one brain there, and real competition waits for predator and prey.

## Open questions
- Should learning from pixels stay out (the default), or be tried on Snake?
EOF

I've written a draft brief at `docs/brief.md`. It's about 420 words of prose and still marked Draft.

- **Problem:** tutorials hand you working code, so when an agent fails to learn you can't tell why. The fix is to build small worlds and write the learning methods yourself.
- **Top goal:** you understand each core learning method well enough to write it yourself and explain why it works or fails. Goal 3 means every agent has to beat a simple hand-written player and come close to the library version of the same method.
- **Biggest Not Doing item:** no learning from screen pixels. Agents get positions and distances, which keeps training under about an hour on your laptop.

**Your words:** "so I can learn RL by building" UR-02 → Goal 1 "understand each core learning method well enough to write it myself"; "No real RL training before beyond tutorials" UR-12 → Who it's for "new to reinforcement learning beyond tutorials"; "a few weeks per environment" UR-13 and "No deadline." UR-17 → Constraints "a few weeks per world, and no deadline". Tool and number choices (your own code in NumPy/PyTorch vs a library, Apple Silicon, the 1-hour limit, the past-opponents pool) are saved for the spec and architecture, not the brief. Open brief requests: none.

**One check on Not Doing:** I ruled out learning from pixels, which you didn't mention. My guess is you don't need it, and leaving it out keeps the 1-hour limit realistic. The default is out; it's listed under Open questions in case you want to try it on Snake.

**Proposed roadmap stages on acceptance.** Each would get the skills `null-hypothesis-testing` (is the agent really better than the hand-written player or the library, beyond chance?) and `dataviz` (learning curves).
- **S1: Snake.** Watch a Snake agent you wrote beat the hand-written player and get close to the library version, with every run saved and plotted. This stage also builds the shared replays and run log.
- **S2: Fish tank.** Watch fish with limited sight, sharing one policy, outlast the "swim straight away from the ball" fish.
- **S3: Predator & prey.** Built on the tank. First both sides learn at once and you watch them go in circles; then training against past opponents settles it.
- Snake algorithm ladder (option 4): **no stage for now**. It can be added later as an idea when you want it.

Stages S1–S3 with those skills [yes / edit]? Then **accept** the brief or tell me what to change.
